earlier.company_overview: Northwind Logistics is an asset-based freight transportation carrier operating a terminal network with LTL-style industrial freight and a fast-growing last-mile e-commerce delivery segment. Growth is currently driven by pricing/yield discipline and new last-mile retail accounts, with two new Texas terminals under construction.

financial_summary.change: (80) bps (improvement); best Q2 in company history

financial_summary.metric: Yield: revenue per cwt ex-fuel / tonnage per day

earlier.revenue_performance: Revenue of $1.42B grew 8.4% reported and 9.6% excluding fuel surcharge, with fuel surcharge revenue roughly flat as lower diesel offset higher volume. The mix of growth is the key point: pricing, not volume, drove the quarter, with revenue per hundredweight ex-fuel up 5.2% versus tonnage per day up 3.1%. Last-mile was the fastest-growing segment at $186M, +24% y/y, on three new e-commerce accounts onboarded in the quarter, with segment margin improving to (1.8)% from (6.1)%. Free cash flow was $142M, capex $98M, buybacks $75M, and net leverage ended at 1.2x adjusted EBITDA.
earlier.yoy_growth: Revenue +8.4% (+9.6% ex-fuel); adjusted EPS +11.4% ($1.86 vs $1.67); operating ratio improved 80 bps to 88.4%; tonnage per day +3.1% though June turned negative at (2)%, the first negative month since early 2024; revenue per cwt ex-fuel +5.2%; last-mile revenue +24%; pickup and delivery stops per hour +3%; driver wages and benefits +6% per hour; top-10 customer concentration rose to 31% of revenue from 27%.
earlier.management_guidance: Management raised both FY2025 revenue and adjusted EPS guidance, with the raise explicitly framed as a yield story rather than a volume story. FY2025 revenue is now $5.75-$5.85B (from $5.65-$5.80B) and adjusted EPS $7.10-$7.40 (from $6.95-$7.30). The outlook embeds tonnage flat to down 2% for the remainder of the year, consistent with June, and mid-single-digit yield improvement, supported by back-half contract renewals repricing at high-single-digit increases. FY2025 capex budget is maintained at $410M, including the two Texas terminals and ~1,100 tractors. Management guided Q3 to be 'more measured' with earnings weighted to Q4 as the Texas terminals open and renewals take effect; the terminals contribute minimally in FY2025 and are a FY2026 story. Marcus Lee also flagged a path to a mid-87s operating ratio next year, contingent on a stable environment rather than a volume recovery.

guidance_bridge.current: 'Path to the mid-87s next year', assumes stable environment

top_risks: Industrial demand deterioration: June tonnage per day turned negative at (2)%, the first negative month since early 2024, and Midwest manufacturing customers are tightening inventories. The raised guide assumes tonnage only flat to down 2%; Whitfield conceded that if tonnage fell materially further 'we would have a conversation.'

Cost/price squeeze: driver wages and benefits are up 6% per hour against 5.2% yield improvement, which management acknowledged narrows incremental margins on pure price. The offset has been density and productivity (+3% stops per hour), which is precisely what erodes if volumes soften.

Customer concentration: top-10 customers rose to 31% of revenue from 27% on new last-mile accounts, and management said it may tick up further near term. Last-mile also still runs at a (1.8)% operating margin, so the fastest-growing, most concentrated revenue is the least profitable.
top_opportunities: Back-half contract renewals repricing at high-single-digit increases, above the mid-single-digit yield assumption embedded in guidance, providing visible pricing-led earnings support independent of volume.

Last-mile crossing breakeven within two to three quarters per management, with margin already improved 430 bps y/y to (1.8)%; the drag was onboarding cost and purchased transportation that fades as accounts move onto owned capacity.

Two new Texas terminals (Laredo, San Antonio) opening in Q4 on schedule, targeting an estimated $600M addressable cross-border and Central Texas market; essentially no FY2025 contribution, so it is incremental FY2026 volume and a path to normalizing customer concentration.

key_quotes.speaker: Dana Whitfield, President and CEO
key_quotes.quote: The raise is fundamentally a yield story, not a volume story. We have visibility into contract renewals for the back half, and those are repricing at high-single-digit increases. Our guidance already assumes volumes are flat to down 2%. If tonnage were to fall materially further than that, we would have a conversation.

key_quotes.speaker: Marcus Lee, EVP and CFO
key_quotes.quote: You're pointing at exactly the right tension, Priya. On a per-unit basis, yes, wage inflation ahead of yield compresses incremental margins. What has offset it so far is density and productivity... If volumes soften, density becomes harder to hold, so we are managing staffing carefully. We are not adding headcount in the industrial-heavy terminals, and we are letting attrition work.

key_quotes.speaker: Marcus Lee, EVP and CFO
key_quotes.quote: It assumes a stable environment. It does not require a strong recovery, but it does require that the current softness doesn't deepen significantly.

earlier.disclosure_reason: Management beat on the quarter (revenue +8.4%, adjusted EPS +11.4%, record Q2 operating ratio of 88.4%) and raised both ends of FY2025 revenue and adjusted EPS guidance, with the raise underpinned by contracted high-single-digit renewal pricing rather than volume assumptions. The tone is tempered rather than contradicted by candid disclosure of June tonnage turning negative, wage inflation running above yield, and rising customer concentration; guidance already embeds flat-to-down-2% tonnage, so the raise is built on a conservative volume base.
earlier.analyst_summary: Northwind delivered a clean yield-driven beat and raised FY2025 guidance: revenue to $5.75-$5.85B (+$75M at midpoint, +1.3%) and adjusted EPS to $7.10-$7.40 (+$0.125 at midpoint, +1.8%), with capex held at $410M. The quality of the raise is better than the headline suggests because it is priced, not volume-derived: back-half renewals are repricing at high single digits versus a mid-single-digit yield assumption, and the guide already embeds tonnage flat to down 2%, consistent with June's (2)%. The offsetting issue is the cost line. Driver wages are +6% per hour against +5.2% yield, and Lee conceded unprompted in Q&A that incremental margins on pure price are narrowing, with density and the +3% stops-per-hour productivity gain the only offset, precisely the lever that breaks if industrial volumes decay further. The mid-87s FY2026 operating ratio path is explicitly conditioned on the current softness not deepening. Two swing factors for FY2026: last-mile crossing breakeven within two to three quarters off a (1.8)% margin (430 bps y/y improvement), and the Laredo/San Antonio terminals, which management said contribute minimally in FY2025 against a claimed $600M addressable market. Watch Q3, which management pre-flagged as 'more measured' with earnings weighted to Q4, monthly tonnage versus the flat-to-down-2% floor, and top-10 concentration at 31% (from 27%) as last-mile scales.

later.company_overview: Northwind Logistics is an asset-based freight transportation carrier operating a terminal-based linehaul network with a growing last-mile delivery segment. Volumes are levered to U.S. industrial demand, with recent network expansion into cross-border lanes (Laredo).

financial_summary.metric: Revenue per cwt ex-fuel / Last-mile revenue

later.revenue_performance: Revenue of $1.39B grew 0.7% y/y, or 1.4% excluding fuel surcharge, with the entire result driven by price rather than volume. Revenue per hundredweight ex-fuel rose 5.1% while tonnage per day fell 4.3%, with deterioration through the quarter (September down 5.6%). Management attributed the volume shortfall to deeper-than-expected industrial destocking plus roughly $40M of annualized revenue deliberately walked away from on margin thresholds as competitors discounted. Last-mile was the standout: $204M revenue, up 19%, and the first profitable quarter in segment history at a 0.4% operating margin, driven by insourcing volume off purchased transportation. Free cash flow was $88M; net leverage 1.4x adjusted EBITDA; buybacks moderated to $20M.
later.yoy_growth: Revenue +0.7% reported (+1.4% ex-fuel); adjusted EPS (4.5)% to $1.71; operating ratio 140 bps worse at 89.8% versus 88.4%. Volume deleverage on a largely fixed terminal network, ~6% per-hour driver wage inflation, and a 12% increase in insurance and claims expense drove margin erosion, partly offset by improved purchased transportation. Last-mile revenue grew 19%, decelerating from 24% in Q2 as new-account onboarding laps.
later.management_guidance: Guidance cut across the board. FY2025 revenue lowered to $5.55-$5.65B from $5.75-$5.85B; FY2025 adjusted EPS lowered to $6.60-$6.85 from $7.10-$7.40. The revised range embeds Q4 tonnage down 4% to 6% with yield improvement of approximately 4.5%, as renewal increases moderate from high-single-digit levels. FY2025 capex cut to $360M from $410M on the San Antonio terminal deferral to fiscal 2026 and a smaller tractor buy. Critically, management declined to reaffirm the July framing of a mid-87s operating ratio for fiscal 2026, citing uncertainty on industrial recovery timing; FY2026 guidance comes in January. Management is explicitly not calling a bottom and is planning for soft demand through at least calendar year-end; headcount is down 3% since June via attrition.
top_risks: Volume deterioration is not stabilizing: October to date is running in line with September's down 5.6%, and management refuses to call a bottom, leaving the cut FY guide exposed to further downside if industrial destocking persists into calendar 2026.

Structural cost-price gap: driver wage inflation ~6% per hour against guided yield of ~4.5%, with density — the offset — eroding as tonnage falls. CFO explicitly cited this as a key reason for not reaffirming the FY2026 OR target.

Credibility: guidance was raised 90 days ago on a volume assumption of flat to down 2% that came in at down 4.3%; the CEO conceded the guide was 'too optimistic on volume,' and insurance/claims expense rose 12% y/y on industry-wide severity.
top_opportunities: Last-mile reached first-ever profitability (0.4% op margin on $204M revenue, +19%) with management stating the driver — insourcing off purchased transportation — is durable and the segment should stay profitable.

Pricing discipline preserved: yield +5.1% ex-fuel held within range despite competitive discounting, and ~$40M of annualized sub-threshold revenue was shed, positioning margin recovery when volume returns.

Self-help and balance sheet flexibility: capex cut $50M, San Antonio deferred, headcount down 3% via attrition, linehaul schedules trimmed, $88M FCF and 1.4x net leverage — operating leverage should snap back on an industrial recovery, with Laredo cross-border volumes already tracking to plan.

key_quotes.speaker: Dana Whitfield, President and CEO
key_quotes.quote: Our July guidance assumed tonnage flat to down 2%, and we delivered down 4.3%. The industrial destocking was deeper and broader than customers told us it would be, and we compounded it by declining unprofitable freight. I own that the guidance was too optimistic on volume.

key_quotes.speaker: Marcus Lee, EVP and CFO
key_quotes.quote: If yield settles in the mid-4s and wages stay near 6%, we need productivity and density gains to close that gap, and density is exactly what a volume decline takes away. That's the honest picture, and it's a large part of why we're not reaffirming the fiscal 2026 target.

key_quotes.speaker: Dana Whitfield, President and CEO
key_quotes.quote: Our view is that freight priced below our cost of capital doesn't become profitable because the network has spare capacity; it just makes the network busier while destroying value. So the principle holds.

later.disclosure_reason: Guidance was cut on both lines just one quarter after being raised — revenue down $200M (3.4)% and adjusted EPS down $0.525 (7.2)% at the midpoint — and the FY2026 mid-87s operating ratio target was effectively withdrawn. Q4 embeds tonnage down 4-6% with decelerating yield against 6% wage inflation, October is tracking at September's weakest level, and management explicitly declines to call a bottom. Capex cut, a deferred terminal and moderated buybacks are defensive. The last-mile profitability milestone and held pricing are genuine positives but immaterial against a $204M segment inside a $5.6B revenue base.
later.analyst_summary: A miss-and-cut quarter with a withdrawn forward target. Q3 revenue of $1.39B (+0.7%, +1.4% ex-fuel) was entirely price: yield ex-fuel +5.1% against tonnage per day (4.3)%, with September the trough at (5.6)% and October running in line with it. Operating ratio deteriorated 140 bps to 89.8% on volume deleverage, ~6% driver wage inflation and a 12% rise in insurance/claims; adjusted EPS fell 4.5% to $1.71, GAAP $1.63 after $9M of San Antonio deferral costs. The bridge is the story: FY2025 revenue to $5.55-$5.65B from $5.75-$5.85B (-$200M, (3.4)% at midpoint), adjusted EPS to $6.60-$6.85 from $7.10-$7.40 (-$0.525, (7.2)%), capex to $360M from $410M, and the July mid-87s FY2026 operating ratio framing explicitly not reaffirmed. Q4 assumes tonnage down 4-6% with yield moderating to ~4.5% — below the 6% wage run-rate, the structural gap the CFO conceded under questioning requires density to close, precisely what falling volume removes. Management chose price over volume, shedding ~$40M of annualized revenue, and reiterated the principle holds with only selective lane-level flexibility. Offsets: last-mile at $204M (+19%, decelerating from +24%) turned profitable for the first time at 0.4% margin on durable insourcing; Laredo is open and on plan; balance sheet is clean at 1.4x with $88M FCF. But buybacks were throttled to $20M and the company is not calling a bottom. Watch monthly tonnage prints and the January FY2026 guide as the next catalysts.

comparison.headline: One quarter after raising guidance on a "yield story," Northwind cut FY2025 revenue and EPS guidance, withdrew the FY2026 mid-87s operating ratio target, and deferred a terminal as tonnage fell 4.3% versus a flat-to-down-2% assumption.
comparison.disclosure_shift: From confident beat-and-raise to open mea culpa. In July, Whitfield framed softness as contained — June tonnage (2)% was disclosed but guidance was raised on both lines with the explicit claim "the raise is fundamentally a yield story, not a volume story." In October, the opening line is "the third quarter was difficult, and I want to start by being direct about it," with the CEO stating "I own that the guidance was too optimistic on volume." Management moved from conditional caution ("if tonnage were to fall materially further than that, we would have a conversation") to defensive action: guidance cut, capex cut $50M, San Antonio deferred, buyback throttled from $75M to $20M, headcount down 3%, and an explicit refusal to reaffirm the FY2026 operating ratio framing or call a bottom.

deltas.commentary: Growth essentially vanished in one quarter; all of the remaining growth is price, none is volume.

deltas.later: (4.3)% for Q3; September (5.6)%; October tracking in line with September
deltas.commentary: The single most damaging delta. June's (2)% was the floor embedded in July guidance; actuals came in more than twice as bad and are still worsening month to month.

deltas.earlier: 88.4%, (80) bps improvement, best Q2 in company history
deltas.commentary: A 220 bps swing in the y/y direction. Driven by volume deleverage on a fixed terminal network, ~6% driver wage inflation, and insurance/claims up 12% y/y on industry accident severity — a cost line not flagged in July.
From double-digit growth to decline. GAAP EPS $1.63 includes $9M of San Antonio deferral costs.

deltas.metric: Yield (revenue per cwt ex-fuel) vs driver wage inflation
deltas.later: Yield +5.1% actual, Q4 guided ~4.5%, vs wages still ~6%/hour
deltas.commentary: Pricing held in the quarter but the forward gap widens as renewals moderate from high-single-digit to mid-4s. The CFO conceded this gap is structural, not cyclical, and cited it as a main reason for not reaffirming FY2026.

deltas.later: $204M, +19%, +0.4% operating margin — first profitable quarter ever
deltas.commentary: The one genuine improvement, and it beat management's own two-to-three-quarter breakeven promise. But growth is decelerating as onboarding laps, and $204M inside a ~$5.6B revenue base is immaterial to the consolidated story.

new_risks: Volume decline has not bottomed: October to date is running in line with September's (5.6)%, and management explicitly refuses to call a bottom, leaving the already-cut Q4 guide (tonnage down 4-6%) exposed.
Insurance and claims expense up 12% y/y on industry-wide accident severity — a new cost headwind not mentioned in Q2.

Guidance credibility impaired: the raise 90 days ago rested on a volume floor that broke within the quarter, and the FY2026 operating ratio framing offered in July has been withdrawn before it was ever formalized.

Pricing discipline now has a measurable volume cost — ~$40M of annualized revenue walked away from — and management has opened the door to lane-level flexibility, hinting the yield discipline that supported the July thesis may bend.
resolved_risks: Last-mile loss-making status resolved: segment reached its first-ever profitable quarter at 0.4% margin, and management states the driver (insourcing off purchased transportation) is durable with no one-time benefit.
Customer concentration stopped rising: top-10 flat at 31% q/q versus July's warning it "may tick up modestly."
Purchased transportation cost pressure, cited in Q2 as a margin drag, improved as last-mile accounts moved onto owned capacity.
Laredo terminal execution risk reduced: opened in September with cross-border volumes in line with plan.
comparison.guidance_change: Cut on every line. FY2025 revenue to $5.55-$5.65B from $5.75-$5.85B (-$200M, (3.4)% at midpoint); FY2025 adjusted EPS to $6.60-$6.85 from $7.10-$7.40 (-$0.525, (7.2)% at midpoint); FY2025 capex to $360M from $410M (-$50M). The revised range embeds Q4 tonnage down 4-6% (versus July's flat-to-down-2% for the balance of the year) and yield of ~4.5% (versus mid-single-digit). The July path to a mid-87s FY2026 operating ratio was explicitly not reaffirmed, with FY2026 guidance deferred to January. Note the net two-quarter effect: EPS guidance is now $0.40 below the midpoint of the range that stood before the July raise.
comparison.tone_change: Materially more sober and more conditional. July language was assertive — "best second quarter in the company's history," "raised guidance built on pricing we have visibility into," "we are comfortable with that trade." October opens with "the third quarter was difficult" and closes with "the environment moved against us faster than we expected, and our guidance reflected an optimism on volume that did not materialize." The hedging in Q2 Q&A ("it assumes a stable environment... it does require that the current softness doesn't deepen significantly") was converted into an explicit withdrawal three months later. Lee's candour increased rather than decreased — he volunteered that the wage/yield gap is "a structural headwind that doesn't depend on the cycle" and called it "the honest picture." Whitfield still defends the price-over-volume principle ("the principle holds") but now qualifies it with lane-by-lane threshold reviews, a softening of the July absolutism.
what_to_watch: Monthly tonnage prints versus the Q4 guide of down 4-6% — October is already tracking at September's (5.6)% trough, so the cut guide has little cushion if destocking persists.
The January FY2026 guide, specifically whether a mid-87s operating ratio reappears or is replaced by something materially worse, and what tonnage and yield assumptions underpin it.

The yield/wage spread: whether renewal pricing holds near the guided ~4.5% against ~6% wage inflation, and whether management broadens the lane-level pricing flexibility it hinted at — which would signal the pricing discipline pillar is cracking.
